title: Norris explains off-track moment behind Safety Car in Malaysia
excerpt:
Lando Norris has explained what caused his dramatic run off track behind the Safety Car during the latter stages of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, with the incident dropping the Briton backwards en route to a final result of P9.

After the race start was initially delayed due to heavy rain – before a suspended start procedure followed – Norris was amongst those to bolt on the medium tyres for when the encounter eventually got underway. Those on slicks found themselves struggling in the mixed conditions, however, dropping the World Champion backwards from his original grid slot of P5.

An early Safety Car phase – following a stoppage for Cadillac’s Valtteri Bottas – offered an opportunity to pit, which both Norris and team mate Oscar Piastri (who had swapped the medium tyres for intermediates at the end of the first lap) took advantage of.

There was further drama to come in the latter stages when, during another Safety Car period, Mercedes’ George Russell pulled to the side of the track on the main straight to retire his car, leading to those behind him bunching together.

This seemingly caught out Norris, who ran off track into the gravel after taking avoiding action around those ahead, dropping him back to P11. The British driver ultimately fought his way back to ninth when the race resumed, while Piastri ended the day in his original starting position of sixth.

Speaking to the media after the race, Norris conceded that the decision to start on the medium tyre had been “the wrong one”.

“There was enough of us that tried it, that obviously looked more convincing than it was, I guess, from the outside and from our laps to grid,” he explained.

“But I think the laps to grid and the inter tyre was a bit deceiving in terms of how much grip there was. I think a bit of it is also the fact we've never driven on the inter before and pushed on it, so it was hard for us to understand if it was like genuine, [if] the tyres were amazing or not.

“That also led to our decision, but in the end we got it wrong and I probably should have boxed at the end of the first lap, but we wanted to take the gamble.”

Norris went on to detail what led to his off-track excursion in the latter stages, with the 26-year-old subsequently summoned by the stewards for “driving erratically under Safety Car conditions, leaving the track and re-joining unsafely and/or overtaking another car behind the Safety Car”. In the end the Briton was issued with a reprimand.

“I swore a lot,” Norris admitted. “It's just I couldn't see from the angle and, from where I was, how much everyone had stopped because of George on the inside. So by the time I kind of looked at George and looked back, I could see them.

“But it's hard when you're directly behind to see if they're going 100, 200, or 10, and they were going 10, so I just got completely caught out. I guess it's my fault at the end of the day, so I was just unlucky with it. Everyone just checked up so much and I just got screwed over by it, that's all.”

title: 'P2 was the maximum we could have achieved' – Antonelli
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli sits 84 points clear at the top of the Drivers' Championship following his P2 finish at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia – with team mate and rival George Russell retiring towards the end – but insists the Mercedes team “still have work to do”.

The Italian started from third on the grid in Sunday's race in Sepang, and chose intermediate tyres for the mixed conditions at lights out – which proved to be the right choice as he overtook polesitter Max Verstappen on the run down to Turn 1.

Antonelli then lost ground to the Dutch driver after the first Safety Car, brought out by Valtteri Bottas beaching his car in the gravel, but managed to see off a challenge by Russell to stay second.

Running in P2, he was already set to extend his lead in the championship by three points when his team mate had his race cut short on Lap 50 with a suspected power unit failure behind another Safety Car – dealing a blow to the Briton’s already slim title chances.

The 20-year-old said afterwards that Mercedes still had “a lot of work to do” as the team had been “struggling", but added he was satisfied with finishing second to Verstappen.

"I think today was the maximum we could have done," he explained. "Massive congrats to Max and Red Bull for the incredible weekend. And on our side, a lot of work to do – we've been struggling a bit more than usual, but still really happy to come away with P2."

Speaking to the media post-race, Antonelli added: "I’m really happy with P2. It’s a result we deserved because we’ve been... Well, to be fair, after the start I thought we could have had a chance to win today.

"But then after the restart, you know, Max overtook me, also George overtook me. Then I was able to regain P2, and then from that point on I was there in P2 the whole time. So yeah, that was what we deserved today."

When asked about Russell's DNF, Antonelli said it was a disappointing result for his team mate and Mercedes overall.

“It’s obviously a big shame for him and the team as well, because it would have been a good result for the team," he said. "But unfortunately we’ve been suffering from this reliability this year. I’m sure the team is doing its best to understand where the issue is coming from and make sure it doesn’t happen again.”

It was Russell’s second mechanical DNF of the season after also failing to finish in Canada, whilst Antonelli had to retire from the Grand Prix in Barcelona with a power unit problem.

Despite his lead at the top of the drivers' standings, Antonelli says he’s taking nothing for granted and the issues they’ve had with reliability impacts the way he goes into each race weekend:

“[Reliability is] why it’s really important that whenever I go on track, especially with things in my control, I need to make sure that I do my best.”

title: Hamilton hails 'bittersweet' comeback podium in Malaysia
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton says his podium finish at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia was “bittersweet” after completing a comeback drive to P3 having at one stage been a minute behind the leaders.

The race in Sepang was initially delayed due to thunderstorms in the area, and the first race start procedure then got suspended as several drivers, including Hamilton, struggled to maintain speed on the initial formation lap.

When the race eventually got under way in mixed conditions, the Briton – who was second on the grid after a strong performance in Qualifying – dropped 15 places having opted to fit his Ferrari with slick soft tyres instead of intermediates.

With the track not drying up as quickly as hoped, Hamilton dropped to P17 to run a minute behind the leading cars on the first lap – prompting the Scuderia to suggest a switch.

However, the seven-time World Champion made the call from the cockpit to "gamble" and stay on the softs instead – a decision that ultimately saw him roar through the field to cross the line third behind Max Verstappen and Kimi Antonelli.

Asked how he felt after the race, Hamilton wasn’t sure. “I think it’s bittersweet," he said. "We had an opportunity and ultimately didn’t maximise it.

"I had a tough [time] at the beginning, but after the race got going and I managed to keep it on track — which, I’m telling you, was so, so hard.

“I didn’t think that I’d be able to get back to third place, so I’m very, very grateful for that and very happy with it.”

"Obviously we had the wrong call in the beginning, which was so difficult and I could see everyone just pulling away," he added. "I could see on the screen it was a minute down, and I thought that was kind of race over for us. But I just kept my head down, the guys did a great job with the pit stops – obviously lots of tyre changes and lots of chasing."

Although Hamilton felt like it was a missed opportunity, he is looking more comfortable in his Ferrari than in recent races.

He told media it was one of his better weekends in red: “I think we did a really good job yesterday. The engineers did a great job, the mechanics did a great job with changing and fixing the car, getting the car where it needed to be.

“And then I think the car felt good in the race. We often talk about execution, I think [Saturday] we executed really well, and I think we’ll go back to the drawing board and look and see how we could have done better today, and we’ll try and take this performance onto next week.”

title: ‘It’s happened too many times’ – Russell on Bahrain DNF
excerpt:
George Russell was left to rue another retirement from what had looked like being a podium result at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, with the Briton admitting that his run of bad luck during 2026 has felt “relentless”.

After running consistently in the top three for much of the eventful encounter – which featured a delayed start due to rain, followed by a suspended start procedure and changing weather conditions – Russell was still on course for P3 amid a late-race Safety Car phase.

However, there was heartbreak for the Mercedes driver when he was forced to pull to the side of the track during that Safety Car period, with the Silver Arrows going on to confirm that this was due to a suspected power unit issue.

“It's just a bit of a shame,” the 28-year-old said of his retirement when speaking to the media afterwards.

“Another failure, when we were on course for a pretty certain podium. It's a tough one to take. It's unfortunately happened too many times this season, and, yeah, this is just where we are.”

As team mate Kimi Antonelli crossed the line in second place behind race winner Max Verstappen, Russell’s non-score means that the Italian now leads the championship by an even larger margin of 84 points. The DNF also marks Russell’s third non-finish of the campaign.

Pushed on whether he feels that his prospects for the championship are now over, Russell responded: “Yeah, yeah, I'd say so. I definitely needed things to… [for] everything to be going my way if I wanted to fight back and, of course, this weekend it hasn't.

“Never say never but, yeah, it's just pretty relentless this season with the amount of things that have gone away from us, that have been outside of our control.”

title: Verstappen ‘incredibly proud’ after historic Bahrain GP win
excerpt:
Max Verstappen was left feeling “incredibly proud” of his Red Bull team after claiming his and the squad’s maiden victory of the season at a dramatic Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, with the win also making history as the first for Red Bull Ford Powertrains.

While Verstappen had looked in commanding form when he sealed pole position during Saturday’s Qualifying, the Dutchman had to contend with various events in Sunday’s race, which was delayed in getting underway due to heavy rain.

With several drivers struggling to maintain speed and falling out of position during the initial formation lap, this led to a suspended start procedure – and when the Grand Prix did eventually begin in mixed conditions, Verstappen was overtaken by the Mercedes pair of Kimi Antonelli and George Russell.

The Red Bull driver ultimately made his way back into the lead, however, and maintained control across a late-race Virtual Safety Car and full Safety Car phase to secure his and the team’s debut win of 2026.

Asked after the race if his 72nd victory had been his sweetest, Verstappen smiled: “It’s a really nice one, after the year that we’ve had and the progression that we’ve made. I’m incredibly proud of everyone, and it’s just super nice to win here.”

The 29-year-old went on to discuss the challenges that he experienced en route to the chequered flag.

“It was very hectic with a lot of different things in the start,” he explained. “No power, so you have to wait for the power to kick in. But then we made the right call with the intermediate [tyres], and after that, step by step, we moved our way forward.

“From there onwards we could do our own race until the end again, of course with the Safety Car, but we kept it all under control.”

Verstappen also took a moment to reflect on the achievement of scoring Red Bull Powertrains’ maiden win in only their first year as a power unit supplier.

“It's incredible,” the Dutch driver conceded. “I think already, of course, we started, and also to win our first race in our first year with our own power unit is pretty impressive.”

title: Verstappen wins Bahrain GP in Malaysia as Russell retires
excerpt:
Max Verstappen converted pole position into victory during Sunday’s Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, which was impacted by heavy rain, featured an entertaining crossover from intermediate tyres to slicks, and saw overtaking from start to finish – as well as a dramatic late retirement for George Russell.

After a delayed start and then a suspended start procedure, as several drivers struggled to maintain speed on the initial formation lap, the race eventually got under way in slippery, mixed conditions – leading to split tyre strategies and plenty of early action.

Polesitter Verstappen fell behind Mercedes pair Kimi Antonelli and Russell on the run down to Turn 1, with all three drivers running intermediate tyres, but he soon settled into a rhythm and managed to pick off the Silver Arrows either side of a Safety Car that was deployed when Valtteri Bottas spun out.

That Safety Car period represented the ideal window for the intermediate starters to switch to slick tyres, with those who lined up on slick compounds getting caught out, and threats of further rain not materialising before the chequered flag.

Verstappen controlled proceedings after working his way back into P1, pulling away from Antonelli and Russell – who had their own battle over second – and navigating a late Virtual Safety Car/Safety Car combination to secure his and Red Bull’s breakthrough first win of the 2026 campaign.

Antonelli was already set to extend his championship lead over Russell by three points when his team mate dramatically ground to a halt on the start/finish straight behind that final Safety Car, dealing another blow to the Briton's already slim title chances.

Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc were high-profile names to start the race on slick tyres, with both drivers dropping towards the back of the grid as a result. However, inspired comeback drives saw them recover to P3 and P4 respectively, and bag a healthy haul of points for Ferrari.

Isack Hadjar dropped from third to fifth in the closing laps as Hamilton and Leclerc completed their charges, ahead of McLaren’s Oscar Piastri in P6, Racing Bulls’ Liam Lawson in P7 and Fernando Alonso in a morale-boosting P8 for Aston Martin.

Lando Norris sat on team mate Piastri’s tail before the final restart, only to lose control of his McLaren behind the Safety Car and run through the gravel, leaving him to settle for ninth, in front of Racing Bulls rookie and final points finisher Arvid Lindblad.

As has so often been the case this season, Audi driver Nico Hulkenberg just missed out on a reward in 11th, followed by the other Aston Martin of Lance Stroll, Alpine’s Franco Colapinto and the Haas machines of Ollie Bearman and Esteban Ocon.

Pierre Gasly almost crashed out during the formation lap on slick tyres, but managed to rejoin the action and eventually finish 16th, ahead of Williams’ Carlos Sainz and Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto, who were involved in a mid-race collision (for which the latter was penalised).

Cadillac’s Sergio Perez was the day’s final finisher in 19th position, given the aforementioned Russell’s heartache, Bottas’ race-ending spin, and another stoppage involving the Williams of Alex Albon, which brought out the late Safety Car.

AS IT HAPPENED

At the end of an entertaining Qualifying session around the Sepang International Circuit, it was Verstappen who grabbed his and Red Bull’s first pole position of the 2026 season, just ahead of Ferrari rival Hamilton.

Hadjar had rounded out the top three positions in the sister Red Bull, but subsequently took a five-place grid penalty for using extra power unit elements, promoting Mercedes driver championship leader Antonelli to third, and Ferrari’s Leclerc to fourth.

Elsewhere, Alpine’s Colapinto and Racing Bulls’ Lindblad dropped to the very back of the grid. Colapinto served a five-place penalty for his Turn 1 collision in Azerbaijan last time out, coupled with a 10-place drop for taking on new power unit elements, while Lindblad also fitted new PU components, resulting in a combined 30-place demotion.

With that grid-deciding session out of the way, attention soon turned to Sunday’s 56-lap Grand Prix, and how many pit stops drivers might need to make given the high levels of tyre degradation witnessed in practice – Pirelli predicting either a two- or three-stop race.

But then, in the hour before lights out, a huge rain shower – and accompanying thunderstorm – soaked the circuit, adding a completely different dimension to the mix. Would the race get under way as planned? Or would there be a delay to proceedings?

That was answered a couple of minutes before the scheduled start of 1500 local time, when Race Control confirmed a delay – the rain still pouring down, and teams sheltering their multi-million dollar cars on the starting grid with gazebos.

An exploratory lap by the Medical Car highlighted just how tricky the conditions had become, as it slid its way around the track and subsequently reported a significant amount of standing water, which meant conditions were not currently suitable to start the race.

At around 1510 local time, the rain appeared to ease slightly, bringing cheers from the grandstands and grass banks lining the track, which only grew louder when the Medical Car appeared for another assessment.

By 1525, F1’s governing body, the FIA, reported that only a couple of corners were still an issue, thanks to a combination of lighter rainfall and the marshals sweeping the track to remove as much standing water as possible.

A few minutes later, it was announced that the formation lap would take place at 1540. This led to a flurry of activity as drivers who had been sheltering in the pit lane and paddock headed to the grid and got strapped back into their cars.

So, some 40 minutes later than planned, the 22-strong field moved away from their grid slots on intermediate tyres. According to Race Control, there would be a minimum of two laps behind the Safety Car before a standing start – subject to change based on driver feed.

There was drama almost immediately when Hadjar lost control of his Red Bull exiting Turn 2 and took a trip through the gravel, before Verstappen and then Hamilton appeared to encounter power issues. “I can’t accelerate! It’s not working, guys,” said Verstappen. Hamilton, meanwhile, reported: ”I’m pressing the throttle and nothing’s happening!”

A few moments later, Hamilton ground to a halt on the start/finish straight. “It’s a software issue [that] we’re trying to solve,” the seven-time World Champion was told by the Ferrari pit wall. He eventually got going again, but was now massively out of position.

With more cars encountering problems, having been lapping much more slowly than usual, Race Control felt there was no option but to suspend the starting procedure and throw a red flag – the drivers returning to the pit lane and waiting for a second attempt at a start.

That second attempt was eventually scheduled for 1633, with the original grid order in play. So, it would be Verstappen in P1 from Hamilton, Antonelli, Leclerc, the McLarens, Russell and Hadjar, who had managed to escape from the gravel on the first formation lap.

The next question was around tyres, and the choice between intermediates or slicks given how much the track had dried up. It was soon revealed that plenty of drivers were on intermediates. However, Hamilton, Leclerc, Gasly, Bortoleto, Hulkenberg, Bearman, Bottas, Perez and Colapinto all went for softs, and Norris, Piastri, Alonso and Stroll bolted on mediums.

“There’s still a bit of spray; I think we have to stay out,” reported Verstappen on the latest formation lap, while Gasly dropped his car through Turn 5, slid over the grass and just about collected it. “It’s so slippery, guys,” said fellow soft-starter Hamilton.

Perez was the only driver to pit at the end of the first lap behind the Safety Car, swapping to intermediates. One lap later, Piastri, Bortoleto, Stroll and Hulkenberg did the same. Race Control then confirmed a standing start, with the Safety Car duly peeling into the pits and setting up the prospect of a thrilling run down to Turn 1.

When the lights went out, with Perez pitting for a second time, Antonelli and Russell charged off the line to take P1 and P2 for Mercedes, while Lawson surged to third and engaged in a wheel-to-wheel battle with polesitter Verstappen.

Hadjar was up to fifth, ahead of Williams pair Sainz and Albon, the Haas of Ocon, the Racing Bulls machine of Lindblad, and the McLaren of Piastri, with Hamilton and Leclerc pushed out of the top 10 places on their slick tyres.

As that tumble down the order continued, Leclerc decided to ditch his soft tyres for intermediates, while team mate Hamilton ploughed on and tried to make it work. A bit of back-and-forth followed between Hamilton and the Ferrari pit wall, before they settled on sticking with their “gamble”.

Back at the front, Antonelli had built a lead of a couple of seconds over team mate Russell, who was then caught by Verstappen and overtaken into Turn 4. Hadjar also made a move in the other Red Bull by clearing Lawson for P4 into the final corner.

Ocon had made some more progress to run sixth, ahead of Sainz, back-row starter Lindblad and Albon, with Piastri completing the points-paying places, over Bortoleto, Hulkenberg, Stroll, Perez, Norris and Alonso – the latter two having stuck with their medium tyres.

“There’s smoke, like fire. I don’t know if it’s coming from my car or not,” said Bortoleto over the radio as he tried to keep in touch with Piastri. Replays then showed that Leclerc had damaged his front wing with the other Audi of Hulkenberg at the start, which lengthened the Monegasque’s pit stop as a change was made.

So, with the race settling down, how much longer would the track remain more favourable to intermediate tyres? “It does not seem to be drying rapidly. It’s weird,” reported Russell, who was gradually falling away from Verstappen and Antonelli.

At the end of Lap 8, and heading onto Lap 9, Antonelli drifted wide at the final corner to open the door for Verstappen. Just as the Dutchman was looking for a way past, slick-shod Bottas spun off the track in the final sector and triggered a Safety Car – bringing the intermediate runners into the pits for a switch to slick tyres.

Mercedes pulled off a perfect stop under pressure to keep Antonelli ahead of Verstappen, while Russell maintained position over Hadjar, Lawson, Ocon, Lindblad, Sainz, Bortoleto and Piastri. Stroll beat Albon out of the pit lane for P1, from Hulkenberg and Perez, with Hamilton, Norris and Leclerc back in 15th, 16th and 17th respectively. Alonso, Bearman, Gasly and Colapinto were the final runners at this stage.

After a few laps behind the Safety Car, the race resumed and the battle for the lead resumed. Verstappen tucked into Antonelli’s slipstream as they headed onto Lap 13 and launched a bold move around the outside of Turn 1, which he completed at the exit of Turn 2. Russell then brilliantly took advantage of the squabbling to snatch P2 from Antonelli through Turn 5.

Around that time, the stewards noted a Turn 2 incident involving Bortoleto and Sainz – the Williams driver tipped into a spin and dropping from the top 10 to 18th position, and the Audi man pitting shortly afterwards with damage. That aided Hamilton’s recovery towards the points, as he inherited 10th before clearing Hulkenberg for ninth.

“I have more pace,” claimed Antonelli over the radio after a few tours in Russell’s dirty air. “We’ll do something different,” was the reply from Mercedes, referring to strategy. Meanwhile, Verstappen was pumping in a series of fastest laps and leaving the pair behind – his gap over Russell above three seconds by Lap 19.

At the start of Lap 21, Antonelli had arrived on the back of team mate Russell’s car. After a look through Turns 1 and 2, the young Italian reclaimed P2 with a smart move into Turn 4. Verstappen, though, was now some five seconds up the road.

Hamilton continued his comeback with a series of moves on Lindblad, Ocon and Lawson, which put him fifth. Piastri was ninth, unable to make the same kind of progress, with Leclerc now 10th and Norris 11th – Hulkenberg nudged out of the points in the process.

Antonelli’s attempts to leave Russell behind and reel in Verstappen were hampered when he ran wide at the final corner and clipped the pit entry bollard. “Check the front wing,” he asked over the radio, with Russell now just one second behind, and Verstappen moving eight seconds clear.

At the back of the field, Bortoleto was now under investigation for his collision with Sainz, while Albon had also been noted for driving erratically – an incident that will be properly assessed by the stewarding panel post-race.

TV coverage then cut to Hadjar, and a heated radio exchange with his engineer. Informed about Hamilton closing rapidly and being quicker throughout the lap, he shared his frustration and shouted that he was “done”. Behind, Piastri was up to sixth over Lawson, while Norris held eighth, as more midfield pit stops took place.

Russell was the first of the top three runners to make his planned final stop on Lap 33, with Verstappen and Antonelli following a lap later – all three taking softs. “Why have we pulled the trigger so early?” Russell commented over the radio, after being told he would not be stopping again.

“This tyre feels terrible,” came another tyre-related message from the medium-shod Hamilton, who had nonetheless closed up to the rear of Hadjar’s car and was pushing to take P4. Leclerc was up to sixth in the other Ferrari, from Lawson, Piastri, Norris and Lindblad.

Fresh from a pit stop, and running soft tyres, Hulkenberg caught the eye with a double pass on Stroll and Ocon into Turn 4. The German was also noted for a potentially unsafe release in the pit lane, though, while team mate Bortoleto took a 10-second penalty for his clash with Sainz.

On Lap 43, the Virtual Safety Car was deployed due to Albon stopping out on track in his Williams, prompting extra pit stops from Verstappen and Hamilton. As he rejoined the action, Verstappen dropped to second, behind Antonelli – his 12-second margin not enough to retain the lead.

A lap later, however, Antonelli also pitted for fresh tyres, along with team mate Russell, returning P1 to Verstappen. As marshals worked to move Albon’s car, a full Safety Car was deployed, prompting stops from Norris, Lawson, Alonso and Hulkenberg.

Disaster struck for Russell as the field circulated behind the Safety Car – the Briton grinding to a halt just before Turn 1 and dropping out of the race. “Ahhh!” Russell shouted over the radio, with his outside chance of fighting for the title taking a huge hit.

Meanwhile, with the cars ahead bunching up, Norris came close to slamming into the back of team mate Piastri’s car under braking for the first corner. He took to the run-off at speed, slid through the gravel and rejoined the queue down in 11th.

When the race resumed, Verstappen nailed his restart to maintain P1 over Antonelli and Hadjar, with Hamilton and Leclerc hovering in fourth and fifth, and Piastri surviving an attack from Lawson to keep hold of sixth. Alonso and Hulkenberg were eighth and ninth, with Norris passing Lindblad to get back into the points.

A lap later, Hamilton sent the crowd wild by passing Hadjar into Turn 1 for third, capping off an impressive rise from the back of the grid. Leclerc followed suit at the start of the next tour, turning an initially dire race for Ferrari into something much more positive.

Verstappen controlled the final few kilometres to take the chequered flag a couple of seconds up on Antonelli, with Hamilton, Leclerc and Hadjar also maintaining formation, Piastri taking sixth, Lawson seventh and Alonso eighth.

Hulkenberg dropped out of the points late on and wound up 11th, behind Norris and Lindblad, while Stroll took 12th in his Aston Martin, Colapinto placed 13th and the Haas cars of Bearman and Ocon took 14th and 15th – the latter starting the race so well but losing out as various strategies and Safety Cars played out.

Gasly was 16th in the second of the Alpine cars, from Sainz, the penalised Bortoleto and Perez as the final finisher. Russell, Albon and Bottas were the three drivers who failed to finish – the former’s being particularly tough to take.

Russell had trimmed Antonelli’s lead to 66 points after victory in Azerbaijan, but his DNF and Antonelli’s second-place finish means that is back up to 84 points heading into the final seven rounds of the season.

Key quote

“It’s a really nice one, after the year that we’ve had and the progression that we’ve made,” said Verstappen. “I’m incredibly proud of everyone, and it’s just super nice to win here. It was very hectic with a lot of different things in the start. No power, so you have to wait for the power to kick in. But then we made the right call with the intermediates, and after that, step by step, we moved our way forward. From there onwards we could do our own race until the end again, of course, with the Safety Car, but we kept it all under control.”

What’s next

The Singapore Grand Prix hosts the final stop of this triple header sequence on October 9-11. Head to the RACE HUB to find out how you can follow the action from the Marina Bay Street Circuit.

title: Red Bull hail 'untouchable' Max Verstappen after smashing vital milestone
excerpt:
Red Bull team principal has branded Max Verstappen "untouchable" after his imperious victory at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

Verstappen's win, his first of the F1 season, was remarkable for the Dutchman and the Milton Keynes-based squad in a number of ways.

Not only does it mean the four-time drivers' champion has triumphed at least once every term since his second F1 campaign, in 2016, but Red Bull also has not endured a winless season since the year before, too.

However, making the occasion all the more significant is that it marks Red Bull-Ford's first victory as a power unit manufacturer, at just the sixteenth time of asking.

"[It is an] amazing feeling," Mekies told Viaplay after the race. "It felt like a long time since Abu Dhabi last year [when Verstappen last won], but in fact, it's only race 16.

"The first win with us being a full manufacturer — chassis, power unit; a first win with the Red Bull-Ford PowerTrains. Amazing.

"Amazing new start for the adventure. So it's great, and it's great to do it in that way, with such strong pace this weekend. And I think Max has been untouchable..."

Red Bull 'very close to the ultimate pace'

Verstappen was the class of the field all weekend at the Sepang International Circuit, and he earned his 72nd grand prix victory against a backdrop of chaos and confusion, caused by torrential rain and changeable conditions.

But, crucially, it was won on merit, something Red Bull and Mekies have been striving for of late.

The RB22 has showcased impressive race pace in recent rounds, and after finishing second in the Azerbaijan Grand Prix by just two-tenths of a second last weekend, the Red Bull boss felt victory was just on the horizon.

He added: "We will take it race by race, but we have shown in Baku we are very, very close to the ultimate pace here and now, so hopefully we can continue for a bit."

title: Lando Norris learns stewards' verdict after Bahrain GP investigation
excerpt:
While following the Safety Car, NOR approached Turn 1 behind a group of cars. Car 63 (George Russell) had stopped with a mechanical problem ahead of Turn 1, which caused the cars ahead of NOR to slow down. NOR explained that, due to the low sun and resulting visibility conditions, it was difficult to recognise that the cars ahead had started to slow earlier than would normally have been expected.

NOR consequently misjudged his closing speed and approached the cars ahead too quickly. When he realised this, he braked heavily and deliberately steered to the left, onto the kerbs and then into the gravel bed in order to avoid contact with the cars ahead. By driving onto the kerbs, NOR had reduced grip available for braking, which further limited his ability to slow the car.

In doing so, NOR momentarily overshot Car 81 (Oscar Piastri), who was directly ahead of him. The Stewards considered whether this constituted an overtake while the Safety Car was deployed. Although NOR momentarily moved ahead of PIA, this occurred solely as a consequence of NOR leaving the track while taking avoiding action.

PIA immediately repassed NOR while NOR was off the track. The Stewards therefore determined that this did not constitute an overtaking manoeuvre and take no further action in respect of this aspect of the incident. The Stewards also considered that, particularly while driving behind the Safety Car, NOR should have managed the gap to the cars ahead and his closing speed with greater care.

The prevailing visibility conditions were circumstances which NOR should have taken into account when determining an appropriate speed and gap to he cars ahead, rather than a reason which excused the resulting driving. The need for heavy braking and an avoiding manoeuvre into the gravel demonstrated that NOR had not maintained an appropriate margin in the circumstances.

The Stewards therefore determined that NOR had driven erratically in breach of Article B5.13.2a of the FIA F1 Regulations. Such a situation should not arise while driving behind the Safety Car, and NOR was required to maintain a sufficient margin to the cars ahead. However, taking into account that NOR reacted promptly once he recognised the situation and successfully avoided contact, the Stewards consider a Reprimand as appropriate.

The Stewards separately considered NOR's return to the track. Although Car 18 (Lance Stroll) was in relative close proximity, NOR returned progressively and without requiring STR to take avoiding action or otherwise creating an unsafe situation. The Stewards therefore determined that the re-join was safe.

The Stewards also reviewed whether, after having re-joined the track, NOR had overtaken STR while the Safety Car was deployed. The video evidence showed that, as NOR returned from the gravel, he had already crossed the white line with at least one wheel and, as such, was back on track. At this point, he was ahead of STR and at no point did NOR pass STR. Rather, STR approached NOR while NOR was already in the process of returning to the track. The Stewards therefore determined that NOR had not overtaken STR under Safety Car conditions and as such also take no further action for this part of the incident.

title: Audi receive huge F1 fine after Nico Hulkenberg statement released
excerpt:
Audi has been handed a €30,000 fine by F1 stewards, €20,000 of which is suspended for an unsafe situation involving Nico Hulkenberg and a mechanic in the Bahrain GP in Malaysia.

At the final stop under the late safety car, there was confusion after Hulkenberg appeared to move off whilst the front wing flap angle was being adjusted by a mechanic.

The German had received a green light, indicating to him to pull away, but he stopped within 0.2s and avoided contact with the mechanic, as part of the team's release procedure, where an additional manual safety check is carried out by a controller.

This controller stopped the car by turning the light back to red, thus stopping Hulkenberg, whose car was found to have not passed by the point under which an unsafe releasre would have been declared.

The stewards felt that whilst no unsafe release had occured, an unsafe situation had been caused by the early release and handed Audi the €30,000 fine, two-thirds of which is suspended for one year.

It means that provided Audi is not involved in a similar offence in the next 12 months, it will only pay €10,000.

Hulkenberg would ultimately go onto finish in 11th place for the fourth time this season, narrowly being pipped to a point by Arvid Lindblad's Racing Bulls machine.

"In response to queries regarding Nico's pit-stop during today's race, we can confirm that there was no contact made between the car and the crew member on the front left of the car," began an Audi statement, issued to media, including RacingNews365.

"While the front wing adjuster remained stuck, the system reacted, and after 0.2s of green light, the red light was shown again to signal the driver to stop.

"Nico reacted to this, and the operator finished the operation safely. The crew member was unaffected and took part in all the team's subsequent pit stops."

The article continues below.

Hulkenberg's reflections

After his 11th place, Hulkenberg wished his best to the mechanic involved.

"The guy who does the front wing, somehow his screwdriver got stuck," Hulkenberg told media, including RacingNews365.

"It wasn't the cleanest stop, but I hope he is okay."

Turning to the formation lap chaos, Hulkenberg described the events as "peculiar."

"It was very peculiar and strange, and it was a hell of a day with so many weird things happening in the race, so there's a lot to take in and digest."

title: FIA vow to launch 'full review' into Bahrain GP formation lap carnage
excerpt:
The FIA has vowed to launch a "full review" into the carnage seen on the formation laps at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

With the start of the grand prix delayed by 40 minutes due to rain, the field eventually pulled away for two formation laps to sight the track conditions, but a number of cars either slowed to a crawl or stopped completely.

Pole-sitter Max Verstappen was one of these, with second-placed Lewis Hamilton falling down the order as his machine stopped on the back-straight after holding the field up. Esteban Ocon and Valtteri Bottas also stopped before the start sequence was suspended and red flags flown.

This suspension lasted for just under one hour, with a software patch being worked on and immediately transferred to the teams as a fix, with the race then resuming without any further similar trouble.

The formation laps were the first time the 2026-spec F1 cars have tried a formation lap in competition in wet conditions, with the only previous wet weather running coming in Pirelli tyre testing or in pre-season shakedowns.

FIA single-seater technical director Nikolas Tombazis explained that the confusion was essentially down to the software "not being tested in those specific conditions" as he explained how the FIA had quickly implemented a fix.

The governing body then issued a formal statement, confirming that the issue "had not been detected by the FIA or teams" until it was too late.

The full statement is available below.

FIA statement in full

On the formation lap ahead of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, an unprecedented combination of low engine speed, low-grip conditions, wet-weather energy management settings and the Sepang circuit’s sector configuration led to an unintended loss of power for a number of cars.

As a result, the FIA Technical Department removed the energy limit constraint in the affected sectors through an updated software release distributed to all competitors during the race delay caused by heavy rain enabling teams to make the necessary changes to the Power Unit before the start of the race.

This issue had not been detected by the FIA or the teams during testing or during the laps to the grid. The FIA, together with the teams and Power Unit manufacturers, will undertake a full review of the issue."

title: Lewis Hamilton explains 'Lego race' replay farce before 'big panic' set in
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has described the initial formation lap of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia as akin to "the Lego race" before "big panic" set in as he lost all power to his Ferrari.

Following a thunderstorm and torrential downpour at the Sepang International Circuit that sparked a 40-minute delay, the drivers finally set off behind the safety car, only to encounter almost immediate issues.

FIA single-seater director Nikolas Tombazis has confirmed that "a bug" caused software problems, compounded by the fact the cars were running at slow speeds given the conditions.

At the head of the field after clinching pole position, Max Verstappen almost stopped on track. That sparked a concertina effect through the field, forcing others to drive slowly as the bug prevented the power from being redeployed.

Eventually, Hamilton, who was due to start second, ground to a halt on the start-finish straight. Another lengthy delay followed as the FIA was forced to update the software.

Verstappen and Hamilton, who went on to finish first and third at the chequered flag that fell three hours and 20 minutes after the race was initially due to start, were able to look back and laugh at what unfolded.

Asked about the complicated nature of the engines, and for F1 to end up in the situation it did, Verstappen said: "That's the problem that we have.

"These engines are so complicated, and a lot of software is implemented, and when there is something like this, that's the problem.

"I triggered it first, and then I looked in my mirror; I just saw...and I was like, 'Wait. Are they waiting for me? What's going on?"

[Article continues below]

Antonelli - 'It was insane'

Hamilton quickly chipped in, stating: "It was like the Lego race! We had the same speed!"

That was a reference to the drivers racing in Lego F1 cars ahead of the 2025 Miami GP and in Lego go-karts prior to this year's British GP.

Mercedes driver and championship leader Kimi Antonelli, who finished second, added: "It was insane. At some point, we were five wide in the straight because we couldn't understand what was going on."

Verstappen then took up the story. "Then we did a lap, and then I saw eight other cars crawling still, and I saw you [turning to Hamilton] by yourself crawling."

Hamilton added: "Well, I had to stop on track, stop the engine and restart it. I've never done that before."

Verstappen then concluded: "What can you say? I mean, that's not what you want for the sport? Hopefully, there is a lesson learned."

title: Christian Horner takes to social media after 'incredible' Red Bull F1 achievement
excerpt:
Former Red Bull Christian Horner has taken to social media to offer his congratulations after the team took its first F1 victory with its own engine in the Bahrain GP.

Max Verstappen emerged victorious from the chaotic grand prix, to record Red Bull's first victory of the season - and crucially, the first since it switched to its own Red Bull-Ford Powertrain.

The decision was taken under Horner's tenure to take the step to become a power unit manufacturer for 2026, with the factory beginning to be built up under him, with the likes of Ben Hodgkinson signed to lead the project.

Since leaving Red Bull in July 2025, Horner has seldom commented on Red Bull, but took to Instagram stories, below, to offer his congratulations.

RBPT-Ford is just the 23rd different engine manufacturer to win a grand prix in F1.

title: FIA issue apology after on-track stoppages cause Bahrain GP chaos
excerpt:
FIA single-seater director Nikolas Tombazis has issued an apology to F1 fans after a startling series of on-track stoppages caused a delay to the start of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

Following a postponement due to adverse weather conditions, the cars finally emerged from the pit lane behind the safety car in wet conditions some 40 minutes after the scheduled race start.

However, as they rounded the track, some cars began to slow down, with Max Verstappen at the head of the field highlighting that he felt as though he had no power.

Three cars were spotted stopping on the racetrack - Lewis Hamilton, Esteban Ocon and Valtteri Bottas - before they fired back up and got going again.

With the field running at such a slow pace behind Verstappen, who streaked into the distance, the four-time champion amazingly came around to lap the field, with the safety car now running behind some cars.

It caused the FIA to abort the start and, after all of the cars returned to the pit lane, the power units were diagnosed with a bug, which required a software update to fix.

Explaining the situation, Tombazis said: "There was a bit of a concertina effect between cars and some cars almost stopped completely.

"That bug prevented the power from being redeployed and for the cars to start again.

"If we had had a bit more testing, we probably would have managed to catch it in time and not to have such a situation.

"Once the problem happened, our guys realised very quickly what was happening and had to work under a lot of time pressure for an update to the software, which was issued to the teams, and the teams had to install it on their cars.

"So all of that took about 20 minutes. It may have felt like five hours for spectators waiting for a race and for everybody else, which is understandable.

"We are sorry about that, but I think it was quite a fast reaction given the problem."

[Article continues below]

Tombazis: Software not tested in such slow conditions

The opening stages of the race around the Sepang International Circuit marked the first time this year the cars had run extensively in wet conditions.

With the wet surface under a formation lap naturally causing a lower-than-normal speed, the power units were effectively unable to keep firing.

Tombazis has acknowledged that the FIA missed putting the software through such tests at low speed when preparing it for its debut as part of the new cycle of regulations.

"The software was tested, it just wasn't tested in those specific conditions," Tombazis said.

"What caught us out was the fact that cars went at that very, very low speed, which was not normally contemplated.

"When problems happen, people learn. Everything you do, from the phone you're holding, everything is based on learning things and improving.

"I'm not saying that no error happened, the bug is, by definition, an error.

"Testing stuff better avoids errors. That's obviously what people try to do.

"Sometimes things fall through the net, and people learn, and you do a better job next time."

title: George Russell 'beyond disappointment' after F1 title blow: 'You've got to laugh'
excerpt:
George Russell has said "you've almost got to laugh" at his bad luck after retiring from a near-certain third in the closing stages of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

Russell was behind Kimi Antonelli during the late safety car period when a suspected power unit issue meant he had to pull over to one side, turning a net three-point loss into an 18-point loss in the F1 drivers' title fight.

It leaves the British driver 84 points adrift of his Mercedes team-mate in the championship standings with just six or seven rounds of the campaign to go.

"You've almost got to laugh," Russell told Sky Sports F1 after the race. "I'm beyond disappointment. So many times this season it's happened; it's a real shame... but just keep on fighting, just keep on trying to go.

"The podium, of course, looked very certain. Solid race, not an amazing race, but a solid race.

"But not the first time, so I'm pretty used to this feeling and these questions, let's say."

Russell: 'I needed luck on my side'

Having started seventh, the early chaos saw Russell vault his way up to third, before getting the better of Antonelli at the first safety car restart.

However, he could not hold onto the young Italian, who was extracting better pace from his W17, and looked to have secured a three-point loss in the standings. Not ideal, but perhaps more than he could have expected before the race.

But for fate to intervene in his season again, as it did so often during the opening rounds of the year, meaning any hope of an improbable recovery in the F1 drivers' title fight now looks to be beyond reach.

"I don't need to say, 'I think it's gone' or whatever, but of course it's exceptionally likely, and that's just the reality," Russell replied when asked if he must now accept the championship is over.

"I knew if I wanted to come back, I needed luck on my side. Unfortunately, I've had luck not on my side, so you know, a three-point loss today, being behind Kimi, turned into an 18-point loss.

"Of course, if the issue was on the other side, it would have been an 18-point gain. So it's a real shame... but that's just how it is."

title: Lando Norris brands farcical F1 scenes 'horrible' as chaos erupts
excerpt:
Lando Norris has branded the scenes on the formation lap of F1's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia as "horrible" as chaos erupted.

With the start delayed by 40 minutes, the 22-car field began to make the first of two tours behind the safety car before a standing start, but Max Verstappen slowed to a crawl as Lewis Hamilton stopped on track, reporting no power as the field passed by.

Hamilton eventually got going again, but others also stopped, including Esteban Ocon, with the start sequence then suspended and the red flags brought out for just under another hour.

Eventually, the race resumed without further complication, with Norris racing for points throughout, and eventually taking ninth following a late scare after taking avoiding action under the safety car to avoid ramming into team-mate Oscar Piastri at Turn 1.

Reflecting, Norris, a fierce critic of the current engine regulations, felt the episode had proved "we shouldn't have any of that stuff."

"Horrible," was Norris's initial reaction to media, including RacingNews365 of the farcical scenes.

"It just proves that we shouldn't have any of that stuff, the electronic side.

"We can't say any more than what we've already said. It is all coding stuff, and stuff to do with how the battery works."

Norris was then asked about the "driving erratically" charge he must account for to the stewards for nearly ramming into Piastri.

He explained that the incident was due, in part, to George Russell's retirement.

"It was because everyone just hit the brakes into Turn 1 because of George," Norris said.

"I was far enough back that I couldn't really see how slowly they were going, and it caught me out."

title: Mercedes boss Toto Wolff 'massively annoyed': 'It can't continue'
excerpt:
Toto Wolff conceded to suffering "one of my worst experiences" as Mercedes team principal following the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

Although Kimi Antonelli finished second behind Red Bull's Max Verstappen after a chaotic race at the Sepang International Circuit for the four-time F1 champion's first victory of the year, George Russell's third DNF of the season five laps from the finish hit home hard.

Russell's W17 suffered a suspected power unit failure, to which Wolff, speaking to Sky Sports F1, said: "I'm so massively annoyed and not in a happy place.

"First of all, you know, we didn't have the speed that we were hoping to have before the weekend, so there's a lot of homework to be done to recover, which I'm sure we will.

"Then the race went against us. With such an advantage: one VSC, two safety cars, you couldn't be more unlucky.

"To make things worse, a PU failure with a few laps to go to the end with George, which is terrible for his championship and not good at all for our constructors' points.

"As much as I love to be here, when I look at the pure race, it is one of my worst experiences, to be honest."

Although Antonelli held his nerve through the chaos, it was still Russell's DNF that dominated Wolff's thoughts.

"He [Antonelli] scored a few more points than Lewis behind him, and I'm happy because he did the job," said Wolff.

"But it's just this overarching topic, the DNFs, that could cost us dearly for the remaining seven races.

"A championship is quickly turned around against you or for you if you have a DNF, and that's why that can't continue."

title: Lewis Hamilton shares emotional rollercoaster during inspired F1 recovery
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton endured an emotional rollercoaster during the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, with the Ferrari driver chronicling his evolving feelings after the action-packed race.

Due to start second at the Sepang International Circuit, Hamilton fell to the rear of the field during the delayed, wet formation lap behind the safety car due to a power unit software issue, only for the FIA to reinstate the original grid order for when the race actually got underway after a red flag disruption.

But Ferrari's call to put him on dry tyres was the incorrect decision, and Hamilton again found himself tumbling through the field with the intermediate compound the right way to go.

However, the seven-time F1 drivers' champion kept his head down, encouraged his team to take contrarian strategy calls and scythed through the pack, recovering to a remarkable third after a late safety car.

Reflecting on the eventual afternoon, the British driver detailed his changing feelings from inside the cockpit of his SF-26.

"Big congratulations to Max," Hamilton said after getting out of his Ferrari. "What a tough race that was.

"Obviously, we had the wrong call at the beginning, which was so difficult — and I could see everyone just pulling away.

"I could see on the screen, I was a minute down, and I thought that was race over for us.

"But I just kept my head down. The guys did a great job with the pit stops; obviously, lots of tyre changes, lots of chasing, and honestly, of all the years I've been here, this is the best race we've had here."

title: Max Verstappen and Red Bull-Ford make F1 history: 'Incredible!'
excerpt:
Max Verstappen survived a chaotic Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia to give Red Bull-Ford Powertrains its first win in his debut F1 season hailed by the four-time champion as "incredible".

After a 100-minute delay, the race at the Sepang International Circuit finally got going, with Verstappen losing his pole off the line to Mercedes pair Kimi Antonelli and George Russell.

Verstappen eventually clawed his way back to the front, and despite a late safety car, he crossed the line 2.307s ahead of Antonelli to claim his 72nd career victory.

"It's a really nice one after the year we've had and the progression we've made, so I'm really proud of everyone," said Verstappen, speaking to Sky Sports F1. "It's so nice to win here."

As to Red Bull-Ford scoring its maiden win in his first year in F1, he simply described it as "incredible!"

He added: "To win our first race in our first year with our own power unit is pretty impressive."

title: When can Kimi Antonelli win the 2026 F1 drivers' world championship?
excerpt:
When can Kimi Antonelli win the 2026 F1 drivers' championship title?

Following the 2026 Bahrain Grand Prix, Kimi Antonelli holds a 84-point lead over Mercedes team-mate George Russell.

No other driver is within 100 points of the Italian, who is increasingly set to become the youngest F1 world champion and shatter Sebastian Vettel's record of 23 years, 4 months, 11 days by over three years.

Antonelli, who turned 20 in August 2026, has dominated the season, but when can the Mercedes driver become the first Italian to be crowned world champion since Alberto Ascari in 1953?

The article continues below.

THIS ARTICLE WILL BE UPDATED FOLLOWING EVERY GRAND PRIX UNTIL ANTONELLI WINS THE 2026 F1 WORLD DRIVERS' TITLE.

When can Kimi Antonelli win the title?

After the Bahrain Grand Prix, there are seven races scheduled to take place in the season, each worth 25 points.

This gives a total of 175 points remaining, which climbs to 183 once the eight points on offer in the Singapore Sprint race are added.

A scenario exists whereby Antonelli could win the title in the United States, which is laid out below.

Antonelli wins the Singapore Sprint; Russell scores 0 points. The gap extends to 92 points.

Antonelli wins in Singapore; Russell scores 0 points. The gap extends to 117 points.

Following Singapore, 150 points will remain in the season, with Antonelli potentially holding a 117-point lead, with 125 remaining following the trip to Austin.

It would mean that heading to the United States GP in Austin, Russell would be required to win every grand prix, with Antonelli only requiring to score eight points, a sixth place.

If Russell failed to win in the United States under the points scenario above, Antonelli would be crowned champion if he simply scored sixth place or better.

If Antonelli is exactly 125 points ahead of Russell after the Austin race, he would win the title on wins countback, as he would hold 10 grand prix victories to Russell on three, which could climb to eight over the final five races.

Should Antonelli win the title in the United States, he will be 20 years, 2 months, 1 day old.

title: Max Verstappen takes historic Bahrain victory as George Russell title hopes extinguished
excerpt:
Max Verstappen scored the first victory for Red Bull's own F1 engine after farcical early chaos at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

4 October 12:23PM

Max Verstappen delivered an imperious performance to win the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia after farcical early scenes at Sepang on the formation laps.

With the race already delayed by 40 minutes after a severe downpour, once cars got going behind the safety car, chaos ensued with Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton involved as cars ground to a halt for the first time they had been run in wet conditions at a grand prix.

Verstappen was able to keep the Red Bull going, but the likes of Hamilton and Esteban Ocon stopped on track whilst a "software reset" was delivered - with the FIA quickly deciding to suspend the start sequence and red flag the race, which had not yet started.

After a further delay of around 50 minutes, the race finally got going in green flag conditions with a standing start - with a mixture of tyres throughout the field.

Verstappen and Isack Hadjar stayed on the intermediate tyres whilst Hamilton and Charles Leclerc gambled on the soft Pirellis, with both Mercedes drivers also opting for the added security of the intermediates.

On the start, Verstappen and Hamilton both bogged down as Kimi Antonelli and George Russell rocketed away to lead from Verstappen as Hamilton and Lando Norris on the slicks tumbled down the order as intermediates proved the way to go.

As the crossover point slowly appeared, those at the front earned a free pit-stop for the safety car being deployed after Valtteri Bottas spun off.

This allowed the field to take on slick tyres all around - but Hamilton did not pit and crucially stayed ahead of the likes of Norris and Leclerc, which would pay dividends later on.

Ultimately after the restart in the dry conditions, Verstappen was rarely seen thereafter and won the first race for Red Bull Powertrains, with Antonelli making a decisive move on Russell on-track to take second - with Russell failing to finish following a late PU failure.

This means Antonelli's points lead is now 84.

Hamilton recovered to third after passing Hadjar late on, with Fernando Alonso eighth for Aston Martin's best result of the season with four points.

Chaos ensures in Sepang

After the initial 40-minute delay for the rain, the field started a planned two laps behind the safety car, but mayhem ensued as multiple cars ground to a halt.

Verstappen was able to keep the Red Bull going as Hamilton stopped and fell right down the order, but under the red flag conditions, the FIA declared that the original grid positions would be used to determine a restart order, which came just under an hour later.

On the standing start, a mixture of tyre compounds were present, with Verstappen and the Mercedes drivers choosing correctly on the intermediates as Antonelli roared into the lead from Russell with Verstappen dicing with Liam Lawson as Hamilton and Leclerc sunk like a stone down the order.

Hamilton rejected an offer from the team to pit, insisting they stick with the gamble, something Leclerc and Norris had not taken, with this decision allowing Hamilton to stay ahead of both rivals after he decided not to pit under a safety car for Bottas's beached Cadillac, with his soft tyres carrying on.

The leaders, all on intermediates, took the free pit-stop for slicks, but shortly after the restart, Verstappen roared past Antonelli for the lead, with Russell also slicing past, with this trio gapping the pack led by Hadjar as Hamilton began to carve through the field.

Leclerc triggered another round of green flag stops, with Hamilton stopping on Lap 32 as the race proceeded until late drama caused by a virtual safety car and then full safety car with 11 laps to go for Alex Albon's stopped Williams.

The entire field eventually pitted but just as the race was getting ready to resume, Russell ground to a halt with a power unit issue, with Norris also going wide to avoid ramming into the back of Piastri.

The race resumed at the end of Lap 51 of 55, with Verstappen fending off Antonelli to win his 72nd grand prix as Hamilton took third after passing Hajdar, who fell to fifth once Leclerc had passed.

Piastri was sixth for McLaren, ahead of Lawson's Racing Bulls machine, as Alonso scored eighth for Aston Martin, with Norris ninth and Arvid Lindblad in 10th.

Lindblad misses on points

Nico Hulkenberg took 11th, just missing out on a point, as Lance Stroll was 12th ahead of Franco Colapinto, as Oliver Bearman pipped Haas team-mate Esteban Ocon to 14th by less than second.

Pierre Gasly was 16th ahead of Carlos Sainz in 17th, ahead of Gabriel Bortoleto, with a 10-second penalty in 18th, as Sergio Perez, on a five-stopper, was 19th and last.

title: 2026 F1 Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia results - Sepang International Circuit
excerpt:
Max Verstappen clinched victory in a Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia that exposed the frailties of F1's current regulations, after the race was delayed due to torrential rain and thunderstorms.

It was Verstappen's first win of the campaign, and continues his streak of triumphing at least once every year since his second season in F1, back in 2016.

The Mercedes pair of Kimi Antonelli and George Russell were set to round out the podium at the Sepang International Circuit; however, a suspected power unit issue for the latter behind the late safety car delivered a hammer blow to his dwindling F1 drivers' title hopes.

Therefore, instead of a three-point gain on Russell, Antonelli leaves Malaysia with an 84-point advantage in the standings.

Isack Hadjar appeared to be the main beneficiary, inheriting third and the final podium position, which would have marked back-to-back trips to the rostrum upon his return from injury.

But Lewis Hamilton had other ideas once the race was resumed, seizing the impetus, and the Red Bull driver ultimately finished fifth behind the second Ferrari of Charles Leclerc.

The conditions provoked a farcical level of chaos and confusion, and underlined the inability of these cars to run in wet weather due to a myriad of factors, including the new problem of power unit software issues.

After a 40-minute delay due to the aforementioned conditions, the field started a pair of formation laps behind the safety car, with a standing start planned.

However, the power unit software issues highlighted caused havoc. Hadjar went off, and Hamilton fell to the rear of the pack. The safety car found itself in the middle of the order as pandemonium reigned.

This triggered a red flag stoppage, with the race eventually getting underway 93 minutes after the scheduled start time.

But with a mix of intermediate and dry tyres, and some opting to start from the pit lane, the order was immediately shaken up.

However, those from the top four teams that were initially disadvantaged, namely the Ferraris and McLarens, eventually worked through the slower cars to lock out the top eight positions — only for a lat safety car to throw one last spanner in the works.

title: George Russell F1 title hopes suffer catastrophic blow with late retirement
excerpt:
George Russell's F1 title hopes suffered a seismic blow with a late retirement in the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

Russell was running in third, one position behind Mercedes team-mate and championship leader Kimi Antonelli behind a safety car when the Briton's W17 suffered a suspected power unit issue.

Russell went into the race 66 points behind Antonelli, and was set to lose another three points to Antonelli if they had held their positions behind Red Bull's Max Verstappen to the chequered flag.

The safety car had been summoned for Williams' Alex Albon retiring and pulling off onto the side of the Sepang International Circuit with a gearbox failure, and his car eventually needing to be removed by a crane.

At the start of lap 51 of 55, Russell pulled to one side, parking his car effectively at the end of the pit lane, leaving him 84 points adrift of Antonelli in the drivers' standings after his third DNF of the season, after the 20-year-old finished runner-up to Verstappen at the chequered flag.
